facts.value: Item 10 - Appendix E - WNC Treasury Management Annual Report 2025-26, to Council on 13 July 2026, doc 29134. About twelve pages of narrative and tables. Read from the saved raw text at papers/E06000062/29134.raw.txt on 2026-08-16 (no PDF fallback needed — the tables came through the pypdf extraction cleanly). Balance sheet in Table 1 (p1) and Table 3 (p3) with Table 4 (p4) reconciling opening→closing external borrowing; debt portfolio composition in Table 2 (p2); treasury revenue budget outturn in Table 5 (p5); prudential indicators in section 7 (pp6-7). The paper is the annual review, retrospective for 2025-26 with 31 March 2026 as the reporting date. It does NOT name a Section 151 Officer or print an officer email address — Appendix E is the technical annex, and the covering report (Item 10 itself) is where an author bylining would sit. Not on disk.

source.title: Item 10 - Appendix E - WNC Treasury Management Annual Report 2025-26

facts.note: Meeting already passed (13 July 2026, today is 16 August 2026). Draft anchors to the next Cabinet treasury monitoring appendix — per para 1.3 Cabinet gets updates for the periods to July and December as appendices to revenue budget monitoring, so the next one is expected on the standard cycle around September/October 2026; exact date not published in this paper.

facts.value: TIES to the basis point. price_book.py 'WEST NORTHAMPTONSHIRE UNITARY COUNCIL' --as-at 2026-03-31 returns 56 live PWLB loans totalling £645,352,614 at a weighted 3.6591%. The paper's Table 2 (p2) prints 'PWLB 645 3.66% 21.86' — £645m at 3.66% with an average life of 21.86 years. Our £645.35m rounds to their £645m; our 3.6591% rounds to their 3.66%. No count is printed in the paper for cross-check, but the two totals and the weighted rate reconcile at both decimals shown.

source.title: OUR file — price_book.py --find and --as-at 2026-03-31; paper Table 2 p2

facts.note: Reconciliation holds — safe to open the email with the loan-book match.

facts.value: CHECKED and closes exactly. On the excluding-PFI basis (para 3.11-3.13): CFR ex PFI £987m − External borrowing £823m = £164m internal borrowing (paper labels this 'under-borrowing', para 3.13, and gives exactly £164m). On the including-PFI basis (Table 3, p3): Total CFR £1,190m − External £823m − Other long-term liabilities £203m = £164m internal borrowing, and Total Debt £823m + £203m = £1,026m ties to the printed Total Debt line. Two other identities also close: Table 4 (p4) opening external £679m − maturities £166m + new loans £311m = £824m; the paper prints £823m (one-pound rounding). Table 1 (p1) GF CFR £689m + HRA CFR £298m = £987m ties to the printed total, and GF external £523m + HRA external £300m = £823m ties. Interest cost avoidance arithmetic at para 3.19 also ties: £164m internal × 3.81% weighted rate = £6.248m ≈ £6.25m as printed.
facts.note: The paper's arithmetic is internally disciplined and the identity closes on both bases. Worth naming.

facts.value: The DSG deficit is named as a live cash pressure and directly linked to the treasury outturn. Section 1.9 (p1): 'This movement was driven by lower available cash balances, including pressures linked to the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) deficit, which reduced the scope to continue using internal cash to support capital financing.' Section 3.16 (p4): the under-borrowing 'must be viewed in the context of the Council's wider cash position... These include, but are not limited to, the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) deficit, which places ongoing demands on internal cash balances.' Section 4.5 (p6) and 4.8 (p6) repeat the point on the investment side: 'the Council was less able to take advantage of higher rates available in the wider market' because DSG pressure reduced cash balances. Section 5.3 (p5) ties it to the £3.5m adverse variance on the treasury budget: 'Ongoing cashflow pressures, particularly those linked to the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) deficit, reduced the Council's available cash balances. This limited the Council's ability to continue using internal borrowing and required a greater reliance on external borrowing earlier and to a greater extent than budgeted.'
facts.note: This is the paper's own causal chain: DSG → less internal cash → earlier externalisation → higher borrowing costs → £3.5m adverse variance and 0.6-point higher financing-cost ratio. Signal `dsg-deficit` applies but the paper does not print the size of the DSG deficit account — recorded as absent.

facts.value: £987m excluding PFI and leases (Table 1 p1 and Table 4 p4). GF £689m + HRA £298m. Including PFI and leases (Table 3 p3): £1,190m — GF £892m + HRA £298m. Original 2025-26 plan was £1,064m ex PFI (Table 1 shows Original £1,064m against Outturn £987m — a £77m undershoot on planned CFR).
facts.note: CFR came in £77m below the Original Estimate on the ex-PFI basis. Slippage on the capital programme is the usual explanation.

facts.value: £823m at 3.81% weighted, average life 18 years (Table 2 p2). Composition: fixed rate PWLB £645m at 3.66% avg life 21.86 years; fixed rate market/other loans (including temporary loans) £159m at 4.34% avg life 2.67 years; variable rate market LOBO £18m at 4.43% avg life 51.1 years. Total fixed £805m at 3.79%; total variable £18m at 4.43%. Table 4 (p4) reconciles the year's movement: opening balance £679m − loan maturities £166m + new external loans £311m = £824m (prints as £823m, one-pound rounding). Net new external borrowing of £145m in 2025-26.
facts.note: External borrowing grew £144m on the year (£679m → £823m). Reconciles.

facts.value: £164m at 31 March 2026 (para 3.13, p3) — 17% of the £987m underlying borrowing requirement. This is the excluding-PFI figure. Down from the £331m of internal borrowing that the 2025-26 TMSS had planned (para 3.20, p4): the year finished £167m more externalised than the strategy assumed. The paper is candid at 1.7-1.8 that this is a deliberate move rather than a deterioration: 'This reflects a managed transition from internal borrowing to external borrowing as cash balances reduced'.
facts.note: Internal borrowing halved on the year (£331m planned → £164m actual). The £167m variance is the story behind Table 5's £3.5m adverse treasury variance.

facts.value: Section 7.1 (p6) Maturity structure of borrowing (of the £823m total): Under 12 months 24%; 12 months to 2 years 13%; 2 years to 5 years 9%; 5 years to 10 years 5%; 10 years and above 48%. Total 99% (one point of rounding). Applied to £823m: about £197m matures/reprices inside 12 months, £107m in 1-2 years, £74m in 2-5 years, £41m in 5-10 years, £395m in 10 years and above. Roughly £305m — 37% of the book — reprices inside two years. Limits are wide: under 12m max 80%; 12m-2y, 2-5y, 5-10y max 50%; 10y+ max 100%. Not close to any limit.

source.title: Section 7.1 Maturity structure of borrowing limits (p6-7)

facts.note: The £197m under 12 months is dominated by market/temporary loans — PWLB alone has only £26.85m due inside 12m (our file), so roughly £170m of the £197m sits in market/LA loans. Consistent with Table 2's £159m of market loans at 2.67 year average life.

facts.value: As at 2026-08-16 (55 live loans, one has matured since 31 March): under 12m 4 loans £26,850,000 at 4.429%; 1-2y 9 loans £73,850,000 at 4.229%; 2-5y 7 loans £89,000,000 at 4.645%; 5-10y 2 loans £15,000,000 at 4.100%; 10-25y 8 loans £49,292,784 at 4.254%; 25y+ 25 loans £381,359,830 at 3.154%. PWLB inside 2 years: £100.7m (16% of PWLB). PWLB inside 12m: £26.85m (4% of PWLB). Weighted rate on the short end is materially above the 3.66% average — the sub-2y bucket runs at 4.28% blended.

source.title: OUR file — price_book.py 'WEST NORTHAMPTONSHIRE UNITARY COUNCIL'

facts.note: Distribution is heavily long-dated on PWLB (£381m of the £645m sits in 25y+ at 3.15%) — hence the 21.86 year average life the paper prints. The short-end pressure lives on the market/LA side, not the PWLB side.

facts.value: £18m in variable-rate Market LOBO at 4.43% weighted, average life 51.1 years (Table 2 p2). The paper does not print the number of loans, the individual counterparties, or the next call date. Section 2 explains LOBOs at p2: 'Market LOBO loans are loan agreements that give the lender the option to increase the interest rate at a later date. The borrower then has the option to repay the loan or accept the new proposed rate when the lender exercises this option.' 4.43% is high on the current curve; if a lender calls, repayment is one option. But without a call date printed, we can't say when a decision might be needed.
facts.note: £18m is small in principal but the pattern across councils (Dexia at Kent/Tameside; KBC at Bath & NE Somerset going floating; Newcastle's £81m of options) means the LOBO market is more active than the aggregate suggests. Named in the email at a general level — no specific call date to point at.

facts.value: £3.5m adverse variance on the treasury budget (Table 5 p5). Budget £8.6m → Provisional Outturn £12.1m. Composition: Net Financing costs £16.2m budget → £19.0m outturn (+£2.8m adverse); Net Treasury Investment Income −£6.3m budget → −£5.7m outturn (£0.6m adverse); Other Investments −£1.3m → −£1.2m (£0.1m adverse). Variance to Period 9 forecast of £11.5m is £0.6m adverse. Section 5.2 attributes the whole £3.5m to 'higher borrowing costs arising from the need to externalise internal borrowing during the year'. Section 5.4 adds that 'although Bank Rate reduced to 3.75%, borrowing rates from the PWLB and Local Authority Lending market remained relatively high'.

source.title: Section 5 Treasury Management budget (p5) and Table 5 (p5)

facts.note: £3.5m of adverse variance is roughly 41% of the original £8.6m budget — material in relative terms. It is the direct financial cost of the DSG-driven early externalisation.

facts.value: 2.7% outturn against 2.1% plan (Table 3 p3) — 0.6 percentage points higher than planned. Section 7 confirms this as the ratio of financing costs to net revenue streams. The paper does not print the underlying net revenue stream, so we cannot back out an absolute financing-cost figure to compare to Table 5's £19.0m net financing costs.
facts.note: Same prudential-indicator name at Table 3 and Section 7 gives the same 2.7%/2.1% pair — consistent.

facts.value: Council performance 4.08% against the 12-month backward-looking SONIA benchmark of 4.55% at 31 March 2026 (section 4.7 and unnumbered table on p6). Under-performance of 0.47 percentage points, attributed to reduced cash balances rather than investment risk. Bank Rate at year-end 3.75%. Total investments £142m at 31 March 2026 (Table 1 p1): under 1 year £99m; longer than 1 year £42m; principal sums invested >365 days limit £20m — outturn £nil (Section 7 p6), suggesting the £42m over 1 year is either non-treasury investments (per Table 1 label 'Non-Treasury & Treasury') or is otherwise excluded from the 365-day prudential cap. The paper does not disaggregate.
facts.note: Under-performance is a knock-on effect of the same DSG-driven cash-balance reduction — the treasury team ran short of investable cash for much of the year.

facts.value: Section 7 (p6-7). Authorised limit for external debt £1,124m against £823m outturn — £301m of headroom. Operational boundary for external debt £1,044m against £823m — £221m of headroom. Table 3 (p3) prints slightly different Authorised Limit £1,270m and Operational Boundary £1,190m, but these are for total debt (external + other long-term liabilities), consistent with Table 3 also including OLTL of £203m. Table 3 total debt £1,026m against Authorised Limit £1,270m — £244m of headroom on total debt. Principal sums invested >365 days indicator was set at £20m, outturn £nil.
facts.note: All limits held. Two limit sets (external only in Section 7; total debt in Table 3) are consistent once OLTL is netted.

facts.value: INDICATIVE ONLY — only the DMO can quote. officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on your Appendix E — the Annual Treasury Management Review for 2025-26 that went to Council on 13 July, ahead of whatever monitoring appendix Cabinet sees next on the standard July/December cycle you set out at paragraph 1.3. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. The report is clearly laid out and its arithmetic closes to the pound at every table, which is worth naming, and this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

A cross-check to open with. Your Table 2 prints PWLB borrowing of £645m at 3.66% with an average life of 21.86 years at 31 March 2026. Our file carries 56 PWLB loans totalling £645,352,614 at a weighted 3.6591% for exactly that date, so we tie to your printed figure at both decimals you show. Not the loan count, which you don't publish, but the two aggregates you do publish match ours line-for-line. It's the single most useful thing we can offer as evidence that what follows is grounded in your actual book, not a summary of it.

The part that most caught our eye was your framing of the treasury outturn. Section 5 attributes the £3.5m adverse variance almost entirely to earlier and larger externalisation of borrowing than the strategy assumed, and paragraphs 1.9, 3.16, 4.5, 4.8 and 5.3 all name Dedicated Schools Grant deficit pressure as the underlying cash-balance reason. That causal chain — DSG absorbing internal cash, less internal borrowing available for capital, more external borrowing brought forward, higher financing costs into 2.7% of net revenue against a planned 2.1% — is honestly told. Most annual reviews we've read separate the two conversations. The Section 4 candour about SONIA under-performance being the same story (less cash to place at the higher short-end rates that were available for much of the year, rather than a treasury management failing) is the same discipline. Worth naming, because reports that connect a treasury number to the cash-balance reason behind it are rarer than they should be.

Behind the outturn sits the shape for the year ahead. Your Section 7 maturity structure has 24% of the £823m borrowing book — around £197m — repricing within twelve months, and another 13% or £107m in the 1-2 year bucket. That's £305m or 37% of the book resetting inside two years. Our file gives you the PWLB side of that: only about £101m of PWLB matures inside two years, so roughly £200m of the near-term rolls sit on the market and temporary-loans side of Table 2 — consistent with the £159m of market/other loans at a 2.67-year average life you print there. Those rolls happen into a market you describe at 4.4 as 'elevated rates for the foreseeable future', and the LA lending market is where a lot of that money will come from.

Which is why the monthly sector data at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity is worth a look before the next roll rather than after. Every LA drawdown from PWLB by month, with the tenor and rate; every publicly disclosed LA-to-LA loan we can find; and where on the curve the market has been most active. It's the same lens we use to build the monthly brief, and it's free.

On the loan book itself, pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis carries the daily reprice of your 55 live PWLB loans against the DMO's repayment curve. Against DMO notice 314/26 PM dated 14 August, the book sits at an indicative net discount of about £139m or 22% of principal — concentrated on two loans, your £125m 2062 MATURITY at 3.48% and your £35.5m 2070 MATURITY at 1.29%, which between them carry about £64m of that number. Those are curve arithmetic — the DMO's actual quote is the only binding one, and nothing about whether a rescheduling would be worth doing follows from us, because that turns on replacement cost we don't model, on HRA/GF apportionment, on MRP treatment and on your own view of the DSG-related cash constraint the paper describes. It's just a number to have visible if members ask. Your paragraph 3.14 already notes that the statutory out-turn on its own 'does not reflect the full economic context', which is exactly the discipline the discount arithmetic needs.

One broader observation on the LOBO piece. Your Table 2 shows £18m of Market LOBO at 4.43% with an average life of 51.1 years. Small in principal against the book but worth flagging in the context of a pattern we've been logging across the councils we've read — Dexia calling at Kent and Tameside in the same window, KBC's floating conversion at Bath & NE Somerset, Newcastle's £81m of options still live, York's lender calling and the loan being repaid — the LOBO market has been more active than aggregate figures suggest. Your paper's Section 2 defines the lender's option clearly for members; it doesn't print your next call date or counterparty, so we can't say anything specific about the £18m other than that if a call comes, the pattern across our reads is that most councils have repaid rather than accepted the revised rate.

One standing observation. Our liability-benchmark work at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis is interactive and built on live data, which matters given CIPFA has Prudential and Treasury Code updates coming. On a £987m CFR carrying a planned £164m of internal borrowing at year-end, the benchmark view against your current PWLB profile shows exactly where the internal-borrowing headroom you're currently sitting on runs out — worth a look on the same page.

On training, four fit the shape of what you're doing. Strategic PWLB borrowing is written for the tenor and pool choice each new tranche presents; Interest rate risk goes to the £197m under 12 months and £107m in 1-2 years that has to roll into elevated rates; LOBO loans covers the option-mechanic and the pattern across councils; and Liability benchmark modelling is the pathway version, which walks through the same view /loan-analysis renders. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find any of this useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free -> https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn -> https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew
